17-311.r: Highest child mortality (then UNICEF report) → Odisha (75 per 1000 live births). 2020 highest IMR: Madhya Pradesh (43), UP and Chhattisgarh (38).

17-312.r: In India more male than female children are born each year (A false); death rate of male children is higher than female (R true).

17-313.r: Highest share of malnourished children (MoSPI, 2011) → Madhya Pradesh (60%); Jharkhand 56.5%, Bihar 55.9%.

17-314.r: 'Youth in India 2022' report → Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI); youth aged 15-29 = 27.2% of population in 2021.

17-315.r: Average age of Indians in 2020 → 29 years (Economic Survey 2013-14); median age 28.4 in 2021, 30.27 in 2026 (National Health Profile 2022).

17-316.r: Census 1991: largest population share in age group 5 to 14 years. NFHS-5 (2019-21): 0-14 → 27%, 15-59 → 61%, 60+ → 12%.

17-317.r: Population under 14 years (0-13), Census 2011 → about 29% (28.67) of India's 1210854977.

17-318.r: Population aged 20 years and above, Census 2011 → about 59.29% of India's total population.

17-320.r: Old age dependency ratio (60+ vs 15-59) in India → 14.2% in 2011 (10.9% in 1961); women 14.9%, men 13.6%.

17-321.r: Persons above 65 years in India → about 5% (2005); 4.8% in Census 2011 → the 5-6% option.

17-322.r: India's 'Demographic Dividend' → its high share of working-age population (15-64 years).

17-323.r: Demographic dividend (UPPCS 2022 answer) → working population of 15 to 59 years, since India's retirement age is generally 60.
17-323.t: Don't reject 15-59 here: UPPCS 2022 accepted it because India's retirement age is generally 60.

17-324.r: 'Demographic bonus' → surge in population of productive (working) age; UNFPA: when working-age share (15 to 64) exceeds non-working share.

17-325.r: Dependent population in a population pyramid → 0-14 years (also 65 and above); working population → 15-64 years.

17-326.r: Dependency ratio falling → working-age (15-59) share relatively high; India's age dependency ratio 79% (1975) → 58% (2008) → about 48% (2021).

17-327.r: To reap the demographic dividend → promote skill development (close the gap between skill demand and supply).

17-328.r: Not an adverse effect of population growth → bigger working population (a favourable effect); smaller holdings, unemployment, less food per head are adverse.

17-329.r: Human resources and development: both links hold → economic development affects population growth, and population growth affects economic development.

17-330.r: Census 2011: 2.1% of India's population disabled; only about 2% of them self-dependent.

17-331.r: Most beggars (Census 2011; Social Justice Ministry, March 2018) → West Bengal (81244), then UP (65835); India total 413670.

17-332.r: Christians in India: 10.7 million (1961) → 18.9 million (1991, 2.25%) → about 27.8 million (2011, 2.3%).

17-333.r: Religious communities ascending (2011): Jain (4451753) < Buddhist (8442972) < Sikh (20833116) < Christian (27819588).
17-333.h: J-B-S-C, smallest first: Jain, Buddhist, Sikh, Christian.

17-334.r: Largest Muslim population (2001 and 2011) → Uttar Pradesh (38483967 in 2011); then West Bengal, Bihar, Maharashtra, Assam.

17-335.r: Highest Christian share of State population → Nagaland (90% in 1991; 87.93% in 2011); then Mizoram (87.16%), Meghalaya.

17-336.r: Largest Buddhist population → Maharashtra (5838710 in 2001; 6531200 in 2011).

17-337.r: Kerala has the highest literacy (A true), but the highest Christian share is in Nagaland, not Kerala (R false).

17-338.r: Sex-ratio by religion, 2011 descending: Christian 1023 > Buddhist 965 > Jain 954 > Muslim 951.

17-339.r: Lowest sex-ratio among religions (Census 2011 data, released 25 August 2015) → Sikh (903); Buddhist 965, Jain 954, Muslim 951.

17-340.r: Highest literacy among religious groups, Census 2011 → Jains.

17-341.r: Average household size, Census 2001: UP 6.5 > Haryana 5.7 > Gujarat 5.25 > West Bengal 5.05 > Kerala 4.73 > Tamil Nadu 4.25.
17-341.c: Book prints answer '*': 1991 data unavailable, and no option matches the 2001 order.

17-342.r: National Literacy Mission (Rajiv Gandhi, 5 May 1988) → target: sustainable threshold of 75% literacy by 2007.

17-343.r: Andaman and Nicobar tribes → mainly Negroid race: Great Andamanese, Onges, Jarawas, Sentinelese.

17-344.r: Bird decline in India → habitat loss and heavy use of insecticides, chemical fertilizers, mosquito repellants (not predators or organic inputs).

17-345.r: Population growth in India → more floods and pollution, less cultivable land, fewer wild animals; 'increase in wildlife' is not an effect.

17-346.r: Ganga Plain → most densely populated part of India because Ganga is India's most harnessed river (A and R true; R explains A).

17-347.r: Progressive population-resource regions: West Bengal delta, Deccan Trap, Tamil Nadu, Punjab Plain and Ganga-Yamuna Doab, South-East Karnataka Plateau.

18-001.r: City differs from village in social values, household composition, way of living and economic activities (all four).

18-002.r: Urban growth indicates rise in urban population, in number of urban centres, in total population and in urban income (all four).

18-003.r: Cultural diversity → element of urban, not rural, community; rural community has we-feeling, territory, self-sufficiency.

18-004.r: Informal ties → not urban; urban life has competition, impersonal and formal relations, anonymity, loss of humanistic values, heterogeneity, market economy.

18-005.r: T.K. Oommen (Indian sociologist) distinguished urban families by income source and changing values, structure of authority, and urban social milieu and social ecology (all).

18-006.r: Causes of urbanization → rural-urban migration (push and pull), more educational institutions in cities, industrialization; not high rural living standards.

18-008.r: Inclusive development (Economic Survey 2015-16) centres on marginal farmers, landless agricultural labourers, SC/ST; not persons in semi-urban areas.

18-009.r: India's urban population → 575 million by 2030 at current growth ('India 2018'); UN-Habitat 2022: 675.5 million by 2035.

18-011.r: India is not over-urbanized (only 31.1% urban: 377.1 of 1210.85 million, 2011) → A false; big cities lack adequate infrastructure → R true.

18-012.r: China far more urbanized than India (2005: 41% vs 29%; in 1950 India 17%, China 13%); poor planning true but not the reason → R not explanation.

18-013.r: Census 2001, all true then: urban population 285 million (28.6 crore, 27.78%), more than USA's total population (28.14 crore); urbanization largely self-reliant.

18-015.r: India's urban population (28.6 crore, 2001) exceeded USA's total (28.14 crore) due to spectacular urban growth → A and R true, R explains A.

18-016.r: Urban expansion → platform for industrial growth, modern service sector growth and better income opportunities (all); cities run on secondary and tertiary activities.

18-017.r: Urbanization rose fast after 2001 (million-plus cities 35 → 53 in 2011); mobile revolution also true (tele-density 3.58% → 78.13%) but does not explain it.

18-018.r: Not true: 'urbanization is uniform' → it is very uneven: Goa most urbanized (over half urban), Himachal Pradesh least (10%).

18-019.r: Both true: urbanization lowers birth rate (better family planning and healthcare access); higher literacy goes with lower birth rate.

18-020.r: Urbanization in India → reduced both birth rate (more education and work) and death rate (better medical facilities).

18-021.r: First Census attempted 1872 (not 1871); regular decennial Census from 1881; urban share 1901-1941 rose 10.8% → 13.9% (not 18%) → only II true.

18-022.r: Moderate urbanization stage → 1931-1961: urban population up 45.46 million (135.86%), urban share 12.2% → 18.3%.

18-024.r: Census urban criteria: statutory town, or population at least 5,000, 75% male workers non-agricultural, density 400/sq km. Physical expansion is not a criterion.

18-026.r: Census Towns, Census 2011 → 3894 provisional, 3892 final (1362 in 2001); need 5000 people, 75% male non-farm workers, 400 persons/sq km.
